To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) proactive communication strategies lead to higher levels of corporate hypocrisy than reactive strategies, (2) corporate hypocrisy reduces consumers' beliefs about the firm and their attitudes toward the firm, and (3) an inoculation strategy mitigates the negative effects of perceived hypocrisy.

(1) consumers are more likely to believe that a firm is hypocritical when it communicates its CSR policies before it engages in behavior inconsistent with these policies, (2) consumers' perceptions of hypocrisy are more damaging to the firm when the firm engages in proactive communication strategies than reactive communication strategies, (3) consumers' perceptions and attitudes are less damaged when the firm communicates its CSR policies abstractly, and (4) consumers' perceptions are less damaged when they are inoculated with the firm's CSR message

proactive communication of CSR policies is less effective than reactive communication and that proactive communication can actually be counter-productive, that CSR policy statements should be abstract to avoid the risk associated with proactive communication, and that an inoculation message can reduce the negative effects of perceived hypocrisy.
